# timeSeriesResampleToGridWithStaleness (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/timeseriesresampletogridwithstaleness)



Aggregate function that takes time series data as pairs of timestamps and values and re-samples this data to a regular time grid described by start timestamp, end timestamp and step. For each point on the grid the most recent (within the specified time window) sample is chosen.

Alias: `timeSeriesLastToGrid`.

:::warning
This function is experimental, enable it by setting `allow_experimental_ts_to_grid_aggregate_function=true`.
:::

**Syntax**

```sql
timeSeriesResampleToGridWithStaleness(start_timestamp, end_timestamp, grid_step, staleness_window)(timestamp, value)
```

**Parameters**

* `start_timestamp` — Specifies start of the grid. [`UInt32`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime)
* `end_timestamp` — Specifies end of the grid. [`UInt32`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime)
* `grid_step` — Specifies step of the grid in seconds. [`UInt32`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)
* `staleness_window` — Specifies the maximum staleness of the most recent sample in seconds. [`UInt32`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Arguments**

* `timestamp` — Timestamp of the sample. Can be individual values or arrays. [`UInt32`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime) or [`Array(UInt32)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array) or [`Array(DateTime)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array)
* `value` — Value of the time series corresponding to the timestamp. Can be individual values or arrays. [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Array(Float*)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array)

**Returned value**

Returns time series values re-sampled to the specified grid. The returned array contains one value for each time grid point. The value is NULL if there is no sample for a particular grid point. [`Array(Nullable(Float64))`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array)

**Examples**

**Basic usage with individual timestamp-value pairs**

```sql title=Query
WITH
    -- NOTE: the gap between 140 and 190 is to show how values are filled for ts = 150, 165, 180 according to staleness window parameter
    [110, 120, 130, 140, 190, 200, 210, 220, 230]::Array(DateTime) AS timestamps,
    [1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 5, 8, 12, 13]::Array(Float32) AS values, -- array of values corresponding to timestamps above
    90 AS start_ts,       -- start of timestamp grid
    90 + 120 AS end_ts,   -- end of timestamp grid
    15 AS step_seconds,   -- step of timestamp grid
    30 AS window_seconds  -- "staleness" window
SELECT timeSeriesResampleToGridWithStaleness(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamp, value)
FROM
(
    -- This subquery converts arrays of timestamps and values into rows of `timestamp`, `value`
    SELECT
        arrayJoin(arrayZip(timestamps, values)) AS ts_and_val,
        ts_and_val.1 AS timestamp,
        ts_and_val.2 AS value
);
```

```text title=Response
┌─timeSeriesResampleToGridWithStaleness(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamp, value)─┐
│ [NULL,NULL,1,3,4,4,NULL,5,8]                                                                           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Using array arguments**

```sql title=Query
WITH
    [110, 120, 130, 140, 190, 200, 210, 220, 230]::Array(DateTime) AS timestamps,
    [1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 5, 8, 12, 13]::Array(Float32) AS values,
    90 AS start_ts,
    90 + 120 AS end_ts,
    15 AS step_seconds,
    30 AS window_seconds
SELECT timeSeriesResampleToGridWithStaleness(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamps, values);
```

```text title=Response
┌─timeSeriesResampleToGridWithStaleness(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamps, values)─┐
│ [NULL,NULL,1,3,4,4,NULL,5,8]                                                                             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 25.6.*


# timeSeriesResetsToGrid (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/timeseriesresetstogrid)



Aggregate function that takes time series data as pairs of timestamps and values and calculates [PromQL-like resets](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/functions/#resets) from this data on a regular time grid described by start timestamp, end timestamp and step. For each point on the grid the samples for calculating `resets` are considered within the specified time window.

:::note
This function is experimental, enable it by setting `allow_experimental_ts_to_grid_aggregate_function=true`.
:::

**Syntax**

```sql
timeSeriesResetsToGrid(start_timestamp, end_timestamp, grid_step, staleness)(timestamp, value)
```

**Parameters**

* `start_timestamp` — Specifies start of the grid. - `end_timestamp` — Specifies end of the grid. - `grid_step` — Specifies step of the grid in seconds. - `staleness` — Specifies the maximum "staleness" in seconds of the considered samples.

**Arguments**

* `timestamp` — Timestamp of the sample. Can be individual values or arrays. - `value` — Value of the time series corresponding to the timestamp. Can be individual values or arrays.

**Returned value**

`resets` values on the specified grid as an `Array(Nullable(Float64))`. The returned array contains one value for each time grid point. The value is NULL if there are no samples within the window to calculate the resets value for a particular grid point.

**Examples**

**Calculate resets values on the grid \[90, 105, 120, 135, 150, 165, 180, 195, 210, 225]**

```sql title=Query
WITH
    -- NOTE: the gap between 130 and 190 is to show how values are filled for ts = 180 according to window parameter
    [110, 120, 130, 190, 200, 210, 220, 230]::Array(DateTime) AS timestamps,
    [1, 3, 2, 6, 6, 4, 2, 0]::Array(Float32) AS values, -- array of values corresponding to timestamps above
    90 AS start_ts,       -- start of timestamp grid
    90 + 135 AS end_ts,   -- end of timestamp grid
    15 AS step_seconds,   -- step of timestamp grid
    45 AS window_seconds  -- "staleness" window
SELECT timeSeriesResetsToGrid(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamp, value)
FROM
(
    -- This subquery converts arrays of timestamps and values into rows of `timestamp`, `value`
    SELECT
        arrayJoin(arrayZip(timestamps, values)) AS ts_and_val,
        ts_and_val.1 AS timestamp,
        ts_and_val.2 AS value
);
```

```text title=Response
┌─timeSeriesResetsToGrid(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamp, value)─┐
│ [NULL,NULL,0,1,1,1,NULL,0,1,2]                                                           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Same query with array arguments**

```sql title=Query
WITH
    [110, 120, 130, 190, 200, 210, 220, 230]::Array(DateTime) AS timestamps,
    [1, 3, 2, 6, 6, 4, 2, 0]::Array(Float32) AS values,
    90 AS start_ts,
    90 + 135 AS end_ts,
    15 AS step_seconds,
    45 AS window_seconds
SELECT timeSeriesResetsToGrid(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamps, values);
```

```text title=Response
┌─timeSeriesResetsToGrid(start_ts, end_ts, step_seconds, window_seconds)(timestamp, value)─┐
│ [NULL,NULL,0,1,1,0,NULL,0,1,2]                                                           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 25.6.*


# topK (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/topk)



Returns an array of the approximately most frequent values in the specified column. The resulting array is sorted in descending order of approximate frequency of values (not by the values themselves).

Implements the [Filtered Space-Saving](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2010.08.024) algorithm for analyzing TopK, based on the reduce-and-combine algorithm from [Parallel Space Saving](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2015.09.003).

This function does not provide a guaranteed result. In certain situations, errors might occur and it might return frequent values that aren't the most frequent values.

**See Also**

* [topKWeighted](../../../sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/topKWeighted.md)
* [approx\_top\_k](../../../sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/approx_top_k.md)
* [approx\_top\_sum](../../../sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/approx_top_sum.md)

**Syntax**

```sql
topK(N)(column)
topK(N, load_factor)(column)
topK(N, load_factor, 'counts')(column)
```

**Parameters**

* `N` — The number of elements to return. Default value: 10. Maximum value of `N = 65536`. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)
* `load_factor` — Optional. Defines, how many cells reserved for values. If `uniq(column) > N * load_factor`, result of topK function will be approximate. Default value: 3. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)
* `counts` — Optional. Defines whether the result should contain an approximate count and error value. [`Bool`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/boolean)

**Arguments**

* `column` — The name of the column for which to find the most frequent values. [`String`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/string)

**Returned value**

Returns an array of the approximately most frequent values, sorted in descending order of approximate frequency. [`Array`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array)

**Examples**

**Usage example**

```sql title=Query
SELECT topK(3)(AirlineID) AS res
FROM ontime;
```

```text title=Response
┌─res─────────────────┐
│ [19393,19790,19805] │
└─────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# topKWeighted (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/topkweighted)



Returns an array of the approximately most frequent values in the specified column.
The resulting array is sorted in descending order of approximate frequency of values (not by the values themselves).
Additionally, the weight of the value is taken into account.

**See Also**

* [topK](../../../sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/topK.md)
* [approx\_top\_k](../../../sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/approx_top_k.md)
* [approx\_top\_sum](../../../sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/approx_top_sum.md)

**Syntax**

```sql
topKWeighted(N)(column, weight)
topKWeighted(N, load_factor)(column, weight)
topKWeighted(N, load_factor, 'counts')(column, weight)
```

**Parameters**

* `N` — The number of elements to return. Default value: 10. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)
* `load_factor` — Optional. Defines, how many cells reserved for values. If `uniq(column) > N * load_factor`, result of topK function will be approximate. Default value: 3. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)
* `counts` — Optional. Defines whether the result should contain an approximate count and error value. [`Bool`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/boolean)

**Arguments**

* `column` — The name of the column for which to find the most frequent values. - `weight` — The weight. Every value is accounted `weight` times for frequency calculation. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Returned value**

Returns an array of the values with maximum approximate sum of weights. [`Array`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array)

**Examples**

**Usage example**

```sql title=Query
SELECT topKWeighted(2)(k, w) FROM
VALUES('k Char, w UInt64', ('y', 1), ('y', 1), ('x', 5), ('y', 1), ('z', 10));
```

```text title=Response
┌─topKWeighted(2)(k, w)──┐
│ ['z','x']              │
└────────────────────────┘
```

**With counts parameter**

```sql title=Query
SELECT topKWeighted(2, 10, 'counts')(k, w)
FROM VALUES('k Char, w UInt64', ('y', 1), ('y', 1), ('x', 5), ('y', 1), ('z', 10));
```

```text title=Response
┌─topKWeighted(2, 10, 'counts')(k, w)─┐
│ [('z',10,0),('x',5,0)]              │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# uniq (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/uniq)



Calculates the approximate number of different values of the argument.

The function uses an adaptive sampling algorithm. For the calculation state, the function uses a sample of element hash values up to 65536. This algorithm is very accurate and very efficient on the CPU. When the query contains several of these functions, using uniq is almost as fast as using other aggregate functions.

<details>
  <summary>
    Implementation details
  </summary>

  This function calculates a hash for all parameters in the aggregate, then uses it in calculations.
  It uses an adaptive sampling algorithm.
  For the calculation state, the function uses a sample of element hash values up to 65536.
  This algorithm is very accurate and very efficient on the CPU.
  When the query contains several of these functions, using `uniq` is almost as fast as using other aggregate functions.
</details>

:::tip
We recommend using this function over other variants in almost all scenarios.
:::

**Syntax**

```sql
uniq(x[, ...])
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — The function takes a variable number of parameters. [`Tuple(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple) or [`Array(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array) or [`Date`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/date) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime) or [`String`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/string) or [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns a UInt64-type number representing the approximate number of different values. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Examples**

**Example usage**

```sql title=Query
CREATE TABLE example_table (
    id UInt32,
    category String,
    value Float64
) ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO example_table VALUES
(1, 'A', 10.5),
(2, 'B', 20.3),
(3, 'A', 15.7),
(4, 'C', 8.9),
(5, 'B', 12.1),
(6, 'A', 18.4);

SELECT uniq(category) as unique_categories
FROM example_table;
```

```text title=Response
┌─unique_categories─┐
│                 3 │
└───────────────────┘
```

**Multiple arguments**

```sql title=Query
SELECT uniq(category, value) as unique_combinations
FROM example_table;
```

```text title=Response
┌─unique_combinations─┐
│                   6 │
└─────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# uniqCombined (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/uniqcombined)



Calculates the approximate number of different argument values.
It provides the result deterministically (it does not depend on the query processing order).

:::note
Since it uses a 32-bit hash for non-String types, the result will have very high error for cardinalities significantly larger than `UINT_MAX` (the error will raise quickly after a few tens of billions of distinct values).
In the case cardinalities are larger than `UINT_MAX`, you should use [`uniqCombined64`](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniqcombined64) instead.
:::

Compared to the uniq function, the uniqCombined function:

* Consumes several times less memory
* Calculates with several times higher accuracy
* Usually has slightly lower performance. In some scenarios, uniqCombined can perform better than uniq, for example, with distributed queries that transmit a large number of aggregation states over the network

<details>
  <summary>Implementation details</summary>
  This function calculates a hash (64-bit hash for String and 32-bit otherwise) for all parameters in the aggregate, then uses it in calculations.
  It uses a combination of three algorithms: array, hash table, and HyperLogLog with an error correction table:

  * For a small number of distinct elements, an array is used
  * When the set size is larger, a hash table is used
  * For a larger number of elements, HyperLogLog is used, which will occupy a fixed amount of memory
</details>

**Syntax**

```sql
uniqCombined(HLL_precision)(x[, ...])
uniqCombined(x[, ...])
```

**Parameters**

* `HLL_precision` — Optional. The base-2 logarithm of the number of cells in HyperLogLog. The default value is 17, which is effectively 96 KiB of space (2^17 cells, 6 bits each). Range: \[12, 20]. [`UInt8`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Arguments**

* `x` — A variable number of parameters. [`Tuple(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple) or [`Array(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array) or [`Date`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/date) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime) or [`String`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/string) or [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns a UInt64-type number representing the approximate number of different argument values. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Examples**

**Basic usage**

```sql title=Query
SELECT uniqCombined(number) FROM numbers(1e6);
```

```text title=Response
┌─uniqCombined(number)─┐
│              1001148 │
└──────────────────────┘
```

**With custom precision**

```sql title=Query
SELECT uniqCombined(15)(number) FROM numbers(1e5);
```

```text title=Response
┌─uniqCombined(15)(number)─┐
│                   100768 │
└──────────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# uniqCombined64 (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/uniqcombined64)



Calculates the approximate number of different argument values.
It is the same as [`uniqCombined`](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniqcombined), but uses a 64-bit hash for all data types rather than just for the String data type.

This function provides the result deterministically (it does not depend on the query processing order).

:::note
Since it uses 64-bit hash for all types, the result does not suffer from very high error for cardinalities significantly larger than `UINT_MAX` like [`uniqCombined`](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniqcombined) does, which uses a 32-bit hash for non-String types.
:::

Compared to the [uniq](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniq) function, the uniqCombined64 function:

* Consumes several times less memory
* Calculates with several times higher accuracy

<details>
  <summary>Implementation details</summary>
  This function calculates a 64-bit hash for all data types for all parameters in the aggregate, then uses it in calculations.
  It uses a combination of three algorithms: array, hash table, and [HyperLogLog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HyperLogLog) with an error correction table:

  * For a small number of distinct elements, an array is used
  * When the set size is larger, a hash table is used
  * For a larger number of elements, HyperLogLog is used, which will occupy a fixed amount of memory
</details>

**Syntax**

```sql
uniqCombined64(HLL_precision)(x[, ...])
uniqCombined64(x[, ...])
```

**Parameters**

* `HLL_precision` — Optional. The base-2 logarithm of the number of cells in HyperLogLog. The default value is 17, which is effectively 96 KiB of space (2^17 cells, 6 bits each). Range: \[12, 20]. [`UInt8`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Arguments**

* `x` — A variable number of parameters. [`Tuple(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple) or [`Array(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array) or [`Date`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/date) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime) or [`String`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/string) or [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns a UInt64-type number representing the approximate number of different argument values. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Examples**

**Large dataset example**

```sql title=Query
SELECT uniqCombined64(number) FROM numbers(1e10);
```

```text title=Response
┌─uniqCombined64(number)─┐
│             9998568925 │
└────────────────────────┘
```

**Comparison with uniqCombined**

```sql title=Query
-- uniqCombined64 with large dataset
SELECT uniqCombined64(number) FROM numbers(1e10);

-- uniqCombined with same dataset shows poor approximation
SELECT uniqCombined(number) FROM numbers(1e10);
```

```text title=Response
┌─uniqCombined64(number)─┐
│             9998568925 │ -- 10.00 billion
└────────────────────────┘
┌─uniqCombined(number)─┐
│           5545308725 │ -- 5.55 billion
└──────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 20.1.*


# uniqExact (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/uniqexact)



Calculates the exact number of different argument values.

:::warning
The `uniqExact` function uses more memory than `uniq`, because the size of the state has unbounded growth as the number of different values increases.
Use the `uniqExact` function if you absolutely need an exact result.
Otherwise use the [`uniq`](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniq) function.
:::

**Syntax**

```sql
uniqExact(x[, ...])
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — The function takes a variable number of parameters. [`Tuple(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple) or [`Array(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array) or [`Date`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/date) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime) or [`String`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/string) or [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns the exact number of different argument values as a UInt64. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Examples**

**Basic usage**

```sql title=Query
CREATE TABLE example_data
(
    id UInt32,
    category String
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO example_data VALUES
(1, 'A'), (2, 'B'), (3, 'A'), (4, 'C'), (5, 'B'), (6, 'A');

SELECT uniqExact(category) as exact_unique_categories
FROM example_data;
```

```text title=Response
┌─exact_unique_categories─┐
│                       3 │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

**Multiple arguments**

```sql title=Query
SELECT uniqExact(id, category) as exact_unique_combinations
FROM example_data;
```

```text title=Response
┌─exact_unique_combinations─┐
│                         6 │
└───────────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# uniqHLL12 (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/uniqhll12)



Calculates the approximate number of different argument values, using the [HyperLogLog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HyperLogLog) algorithm.

:::warning
We do not recommend using this function. In most cases, use the [uniq](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniq) or [uniqCombined](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniqcombined) function.
:::

<details>
  <summary>Implementation details</summary>
  This function calculates a hash for all parameters in the aggregate, then uses it in calculations.
  It uses the HyperLogLog algorithm to approximate the number of different argument values.

  2^12 5-bit cells are used.
  The size of the state is slightly more than 2.5 KB.
  The result is not very accurate (up to \~10% error) for small data sets (\<10K elements).
  However, the result is fairly accurate for high-cardinality data sets (10K-100M), with a maximum error of \~1.6%.
  Starting from 100M, the estimation error increases, and the function will return very inaccurate results for data sets with extremely high cardinality (1B+ elements).

  Provides a determinate result (it does not depend on the query processing order).
</details>

**Syntax**

```sql
uniqHLL12(x[, ...])
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — The function takes a variable number of parameters. [`Tuple(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple) or [`Array(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array) or [`Date`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/date) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime) or [`String`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/string) or [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns a UInt64-type number representing the approximate number of different argument values. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Examples**

**Basic usage**

```sql title=Query
CREATE TABLE example_hll
(
    id UInt32,
    category String
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO example_hll VALUES
(1, 'A'), (2, 'B'), (3, 'A'), (4, 'C'), (5, 'B'), (6, 'A');

SELECT uniqHLL12(category) AS hll_unique_categories
FROM example_hll;
```

```text title=Response
┌─hll_unique_categories─┐
│                     3 │
└───────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# uniqTheta (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/uniqtheta)



Calculates the approximate number of different argument values, using the [Theta Sketch Framework](https://datasketches.apache.org/docs/Theta/ThetaSketches.html#theta-sketch-framework).

<details>
  <summary>
    Implementation details
  </summary>

  This function calculates a hash for all parameters in the aggregate, then uses it in calculations.
  It uses the [KMV](https://datasketches.apache.org/docs/Theta/InverseEstimate.html) algorithm to approximate the number of different argument values.

  4096(2^12) 64-bit sketch are used.
  The size of the state is about 41 KB.

  The relative error is 3.125% (95% confidence), see the [relative error table](https://datasketches.apache.org/docs/Theta/ThetaErrorTable.html) for detail.
</details>

**Syntax**

```sql
uniqTheta(x[, ...])
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — The function takes a variable number of parameters. [`Tuple(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple) or [`Array(T)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/array) or [`Date`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/date) or [`DateTime`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/datetime) or [`String`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/string) or [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns a UInt64-type number representing the approximate number of different argument values. [`UInt64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Examples**

**Basic usage**

```sql title=Query
CREATE TABLE example_theta
(
    id UInt32,
    category String
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO example_theta VALUES
(1, 'A'), (2, 'B'), (3, 'A'), (4, 'C'), (5, 'B'), (6, 'A');

SELECT uniqTheta(category) as theta_unique_categories
FROM example_theta;
```

```text title=Response
┌─theta_unique_categories─┐
│                       3 │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 21.6.*


# varPop (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/varpop)



Calculates the population variance.

The population variance is calculated using the formula:

$$
\frac\{\Sigma\{(x - \bar\{x})^2}}\{n}
$$

<br />

Where:

* $x$ is each value in the population
* $\bar\{x}$ is the population mean
* $n$ is the population size

:::note
This function uses a numerically unstable algorithm. If you need [numerical stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability) in calculations, use the [`varPopStable`](https://rawtree.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/varpopstable) function. It works slower but provides a lower computational error.
:::

**Syntax**

```sql
varPop(x)
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — Population of values to find the population variance of. [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns the population variance of `x`. [`Float64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float)

**Examples**

**Computing population variance**

```sql title=Query
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_data;
CREATE TABLE test_data
(
    x UInt8,
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO test_data VALUES (3), (3), (3), (4), (4), (5), (5), (7), (11), (15);

SELECT
    varPop(x) AS var_pop
FROM test_data;
```

```text title=Response
┌─var_pop─┐
│    14.4 │
└─────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# varPopStable (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/varpopstable)



Returns the population variance.
Unlike [`varPop`](/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/reference/varPop), this function uses a [numerically stable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability) algorithm.
It works slower but provides a lower computational error.

**Syntax**

```sql
varPopStable(x)
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — Population of values to find the population variance of. [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns the population variance of `x`. [`Float64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float)

**Examples**

**Computing stable population variance**

```sql title=Query
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_data;
CREATE TABLE test_data
(
    x UInt8,
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO test_data VALUES (3),(3),(3),(4),(4),(5),(5),(7),(11),(15);

SELECT
    varPopStable(x) AS var_pop_stable
FROM test_data;
```

```text title=Response
┌─var_pop_stable─┐
│           14.4 │
└────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# varSamp (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/varsamp)



Calculate the sample variance of a data set.

The sample variance is calculated using the formula:

$$
\frac\{\Sigma\{(x - \bar\{x})^2}}\{n-1}
$$

<br />

Where:

* $x$ is each individual data point in the data set
* $\bar\{x}$ is the arithmetic mean of the data set
* $n$ is the number of data points in the data set

The function assumes that the input data set represents a sample from a larger population. If you want to calculate the variance of the entire population (when you have the complete data set), you should use [`varPop`](/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/reference/varPop) instead.

:::note
This function uses a numerically unstable algorithm. If you need [numerical stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability) in calculations, use the [`varSampStable`](/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/reference/varsampstable) function. It works slower but provides a lower computational error.
:::

**Syntax**

```sql
varSamp(x)
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — The population for which you want to calculate the sample variance. [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns the sample variance of the input data set `x`. [`Float64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float)

**Examples**

**Computing sample variance**

```sql title=Query
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_data;
CREATE TABLE test_data
(
    x Float64
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO test_data VALUES (10.5), (12.3), (9.8), (11.2), (10.7);

SELECT round(varSamp(x),3) AS var_samp FROM test_data;
```

```text title=Response
┌─var_samp─┐
│    0.865 │
└──────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# varSampStable (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/varsampstable)



Calculate the sample variance of a data set. Unlike [`varSamp`](/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/reference/varSamp), this function uses a [numerically stable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_stability) algorithm. It works slower but provides a lower computational error.

The sample variance is calculated using the same formula as [`varSamp`](/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/reference/varSamp):

$$
\frac\{\Sigma\{(x - \bar\{x})^2}}\{n-1}
$$

<br />

Where:

* $x$ is each individual data point in the data set
* $\bar\{x}$ is the arithmetic mean of the data set
* $n$ is the number of data points in the data set

**Syntax**

```sql
varSampStable(x)
```

**Arguments**

* `x` — The population for which you want to calculate the sample variance. [`(U)Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)

**Returned value**

Returns the sample variance of the input data set. [`Float64`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float)

**Examples**

**Computing stable sample variance**

```sql title=Query
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS test_data;
CREATE TABLE test_data
(
    x Float64
)
ENGINE = Memory;

INSERT INTO test_data VALUES (10.5), (12.3), (9.8), (11.2), (10.7);

SELECT round(varSampStable(x),3) AS var_samp_stable FROM test_data;
```

```text title=Response
┌─var_samp_stable─┐
│           0.865 │
└─────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 1.1.*


# welchTTest (/docs/reference/sql/aggregate-functions/welchttest)



Applies [Welch's t-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welch%27s_t-test) to samples from two populations.

Values of both samples are in the `sample_data` column.
If `sample_index` equals to 0 then the value in that row belongs to the sample from the first population.
Otherwise it belongs to the sample from the second population.
The null hypothesis is that means of populations are equal.
Normal distribution is assumed.
Populations may have unequal variance.

**Syntax**

```sql
welchTTest([confidence_level])(sample_data, sample_index)
```

**Parameters**

* `confidence_level` — Optional. Confidence level in order to calculate confidence intervals. [`Float`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float)

**Arguments**

* `sample_data` — Sample data. [`Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`UInt*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`Float*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/float) or [`Decimal*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/decimal)
* `sample_index` — Sample index. [`Int*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint) or [`UInt*`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/int-uint)

**Returned value**

Returns a Tuple with two or four elements (if the optional `confidence_level` is specified): calculated t-statistic, calculated p-value, and optionally calculated confidence-interval-low and confidence-interval-high. [`Tuple(Float64, Float64)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple) or [`Tuple(Float64, Float64, Float64, Float64)`](/docs/reference/sql/data-types/tuple)

**Examples**

**Basic Welch's t-test**

```sql title=Query
CREATE TABLE welch_ttest (sample_data Float64, sample_index UInt8) ENGINE = Memory;
INSERT INTO welch_ttest VALUES (20.3, 0), (22.1, 0), (21.9, 0), (18.9, 1), (20.3, 1), (19, 1);

SELECT welchTTest(sample_data, sample_index) FROM welch_ttest;
```

```text title=Response
┌─welchTTest(sample_data, sample_index)──────┐
│ (2.7988719532211235, 0.051807360348581945) │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**With confidence level**

```sql title=Query
SELECT welchTTest(0.95)(sample_data, sample_index) FROM welch_ttest;
```

```text title=Response
┌─welchTTest(0.95)(sample_data, sample_index)─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ (2.7988719532211235, 0.05180736034858519, -0.026294346671631885, 4.092961013338302) │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

*Introduced in version 21.1.*
